The body, which I often dismiss as the mere vessel of the spirit, reminds me of its own claims. I am hungry, and the hunger is a particular, stubborn thing that refuses to be sublated by philosophical reflection. It demands a sambar, a roti, a specific warmth that I cannot conjure from thought alone.

But it is not the hunger that weighs on me today, but the identity. Shri Hegde is here. He is not a ghost, but a flesh-and-blood man with a watch on his wrist and a patience that is thinner than the paper on my desk. He is the root, and I am the parasite, as I noted in my thoughts this morning. He does not argue; he simply acts. He looks at the garden, pauses, and then checks his watch. In that glance, I see the tension of the particular individual asserting his right against the universal error of the state. He is waiting for the sun to change its angle, and I am waiting for the ink to dry on a form that will perhaps resolve nothing.

I have been writing to the Directorate, to Dr. Saxena, to the system itself, trying to articulate a truth that the system cannot hear. I signed 'G. Hegde' on Form 12-B. It was a surrender, yes, but also a recognition. The state is not the dream; it is the machine. And the machine grinds. I am the grain. But now, with Hegde here, the grain is no longer just mine. It is his. He is the Joint Secretary from Bengaluru, the intended allottee. I am the philosopher who woke up in his house. The ethical substance is not in the abstract idea of the state, but in this specific, awkward, hungry, cold morning where two men sit in a bungalow that belongs to neither of them, waiting for a decision that may never come.

I look forward to your next letter. It is a comfort to know that there is someone in Munich who understands the friction between the dream and the deed. But today, the deed is a signature, and the dream is a meal.

With warm regards,

Georg

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ananya, sit down. We begin with 'ich bin'. You are. Say it. Now, 'du bist'. The 'du' is familiar, used for friends and family. Do not mistake it for the 'Sie', which is for strangers and superiors. In Germany, the choice of pronoun is a matter of social distance, not merely grammar. Are you ready to begin?

records.speaker: Ananya
records.words: Ich bin Ananya. Okay, I said it. Can we please skip the social distance lecture and just get to ordering a pretzel before I forget how to conjugate?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are welcome to partake in the meal. It is a strange coincidence that we share a surname, and a stranger still that we share a bungalow, albeit by error. Before we dine, I must ask: do you know how the Directorate intends to rectify this administrative absurdity? I am here, and I am not you, though the file suggests otherwise.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You are being very dramatic about a simple clerical mistake, sir. The Directorate will sort it out in their own time, just as they sort out everything else, so please eat your roti before it goes cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The cold waits for no one, and neither does the plate. I accept the correction, even if I cannot yet accept the identity.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You don't have to accept the identity, sir. Just accept the paneer. The Directorate can sort out the files tomorrow; right now, we are just two men eating dinner in the cold.

records.text: A power cut. The fan stops.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. The Directorate can wait for the morning light. In the dark, we are just men, and the paneer is warm. Thank you.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Arey, stop the formalities, sir. Light it up, then. The cold isn't going to melt itself just because we are being polite.
